items.title: Anthropic ships OpenTelemetry export for Claude traces, wired into 12 observability platforms
items.summary: Now in beta: Messages API calls, Sessions API requests, and Managed Agents runs can export spans via OpenTelemetry instead of a bespoke logging pipe, with first-party setup docs for 12 partner platforms (Arize AI, Braintrust, Databricks, Datadog, Grafana Cloud, Honeycomb, Langfuse, LangSmith, New Relic, PostHog, Sentry, Splunk) plus any other OTLP-compatible tool.
items.why: If you're running agents past the prototype stage, this is the difference between grepping stdout and watching latency and cost per step in a dashboard you already use.
items.action: Point the OTel exporter at whatever observability stack you already run and trace one of your longer agent loops end to end, see where the time and tokens actually go.

eval.reason: Genuine new capability (OTel export for Messages API and Managed Agents); not previously covered.

items.title: Kong built a PR-review agent, and the triage step cut median cost more than the model swap did
items.summary: Kong's engineering blog walks through an internal PR-review agent: running the bulk of reviews on a cheaper open-weight model instead of a frontier model cuts per-review model cost roughly 7x, but the bigger lever was a cheap triage pass that routes only the PRs needing deep review to the expensive model, cutting the median review cost by more than a third.
items.why: Most "we switched to a cheaper model" posts skip the part where the real savings came from routing, not the model choice alone.
items.action: If you're running anything multi-step on a frontier model by default, the triage-then-escalate pattern here is worth copying before you reach for a cheaper model everywhere.

eval.reason: Concrete internal case study with real before/after cost numbers; not a duplicate.
Re-fetched Kong's own engineering blog fresh.
Model-cost and median-review-cost figures verified word-for-word; the post attributes the cost drop specifically to the triage step, which the summary reflects.
Not a SHIPPED item.
Concrete and immediately copyable routing pattern.

items.title: Simon Willison does the math on what Anthropic's distillation crackdown says about rival labs' spending
items.summary: Reacting to a Financial Times report that Anthropic told investors distillation (rivals training on Anthropic's own model outputs) accounts for 5-7% of its revenue, Willison runs a back-of-envelope estimate using Q2 revenue ($11.5B): that's more than half a billion dollars spent by other labs distilling Anthropic's models, if true. The FT separately reports Anthropic's Q3 revenue rose nearly 50% to $16.8B.
items.why: The 5-7%-of-revenue figure is the real signal: distillation from a frontier lab is now a line item big enough that Anthropic is explaining it to investors.
items.action: Worth doing this same back-of-envelope check yourself whenever a model undercuts a frontier lab on price: how much of that gap is plausibly explained by distilling the thing it's undercutting.

eval.reason: Real discourse with an actual reported figure and a worked angle, not a meme or pure reaction; not previously covered.
Tweet and the underlying report both re-checked live.
Quoted figures verified against the post text directly; explicitly flagged that the half-billion estimate is the author's own math, not a reported figure.
Not a SHIPPED item.
Concrete where-do-I-use-this angle, not pure discourse.

items.title: Stanford's Hazy Research lab claims 10-31x faster generation and 4-5x fewer training tokens with a new method (NCM)
items.summary: The lab's post describes a new language-modeling method (NCM): 10-31x faster text generation versus a baseline (21x on LM1B, 10x on OpenWebText, up to 31x on XSum, all on one H100), plus 4-5x fewer tokens needed to train it in the first place. Paper and code are both public.
items.why: If the inference-speed numbers hold up outside the paper's own benchmarks, cheaper/faster generation at this scale changes the economics of anything that calls a model in a loop, agents included.
items.action: Worth reading the arXiv method section directly, not just the blog post, before deciding whether any of it is worth reproducing.

eval.reason: Concrete reproducible research with public code and paper; not previously covered.
Reachable; only a cached copy was available on the final re-check rather than a fresh live fetch (minor caveat).

Re-fetched the blog post fresh at the eval gate and found the 10-31x figure is for generation/inference speed, not training convergence as first drafted -- corrected the title and summary before publishing rather than leave a mischaracterized (if still impressive) claim.
Not a SHIPPED item.
Directly relevant to anyone iterating on training cost and time.

items.title: Anthropic's CJ Avilla and Harrison Stall: why one agent isn't enough, and how Flows runs up to 1,000 of them
items.summary: A hands-on conference workshop introducing Flows in Claude Managed Agents: hand Claude a goal and it plans and runs its own multi-agent topology through the API. Covers why single agents fail (laziness, self-preference bias, goal drift), a live demo, and running agents safely at scale (budgets, interrupts, credential vaults, network lockdown).
items.why: This is Anthropic's own team explaining the failure modes that push you from one agent to an orchestrated topology, plus the actual safety controls, not just the happy-path demo.
items.action: About 1h40m; the core walkthrough/demo and the agent-safety-at-scale chapter near the end are the two dense sections if you want to skip to those.

eval.reason: First-party Anthropic team explaining a new feature plus real failure-mode and safety content; not previously covered.
Video confirmed live.

items.title: Langfuse's Doneyli De Jesus and Annabell Schafer: evals for high-stakes agents, walked through on a banking assistant
items.summary: A conference workshop on evaluating agents where mistakes are expensive: tracing with PII masking, building eval datasets from real traces, turning domain-expert comments into failure modes, choosing between LLM-as-judge and code evaluators, and CI that blocks a prompt change when scores drop.
items.why: Most eval content stays abstract; this one is an actual end-to-end loop on a regulated-industry example, the harder and more useful version of the topic.
items.action: About 54 minutes; the tracing/PII-masking demo and the CI-gate section are the two most concrete chapters if you want to skip to those.
